candidates.printedLatin: Horum autem rationem hoc loco ostendere jam volumus, de quibus quod nobis rectius videbatur alias jam diximus.
candidates.englishAsRendered: But the reason of these we now wish to set forth in this place, concerning which we have already said elsewhere what seemed to us more correct.
candidates.whyContradiction: The clause immediately explains itself with 'alias jam diximus' ('we have already said elsewhere') as a reason for NOT treating the matter here, and four sentences earlier Richard already wrote 'alio loco jam diximus' about the same twelve-tribes material — a refusal to re-expound, not a stated wish to expound it now.

candidates.printedLatin: Ipsum cui noluit hoc opus ascribere, maluit designare ex descriptione.
candidates.englishAsRendered: The very one to whom he was unwilling to ascribe this work, he preferred to designate by a description.
candidates.conjecture: voluit (or noluit sibi for noluit... cui, i.e. the negation belongs to ascribing the work to himself, not to God)
candidates.whyContradiction: The whole surrounding argument (the Psalmist saying 'haec mutatio dexterae Excelsi' rather than simply 'haec mutatio Dei') is that he refused to ascribe the change to HIMSELF and went out of his way to name God as elaborately as possible — 'noluit... ascribere' as printed makes him unwilling to credit God, exactly reversing the point the next two sentences drive home ('Non sibi sufficere potuit ut diceret haec mutatio Dei... Excelsum dicit qui hoc fecit').

candidates.printedLatin: Moeror pro nobis aeternis, mare est a dextris; moeror pro malis aeternis, mare est a sinistris.
candidates.englishAsRendered: Sorrow for us eternal ones is the sea on the right hand; sorrow for eternal evils is the sea on the left hand.
candidates.whyContradiction: The sentence is built as a paired scheme — sorrow for eternal GOODS on the right vs. sorrow for eternal EVILS on the left — matching the chapter head 'De gemina cordis compunctione' and echoed two sentences later, 'ut... mala diluamus aeterna et... bona mercemur aeterna.' Printed 'nobis' ('for us') breaks the good/evil antithesis the passage otherwise sustains; 'bonis' is one letter away.

candidates.printedLatin: Illic ergo praecedat, ut viam ostendat.
candidates.englishAsRendered: There, then, let it go before, that it may show the way.
candidates.whyContradiction: The immediately preceding sentence in the same paragraph has just argued the opposite of what 'Illic' claims: 'jubemur turbam non arcam praemittere' (beyond Jordan we are bidden to send the THRONG, not the ark, ahead) — and the chapter's whole scheme has the ark going before only 'citra Jordanem' / 'ad nostra' (this side) while beyond Jordan ('ultra Jordanem' / 'illic') it follows. Ending the chapter by having the ark go before precisely where 'Illic' places it reverses the thesis the paragraph just built; 'Hic' would restore it.

candidates.printedLatin: ut per invisibilem formam, invisibiliumque figuram, in intellectibilium intelligentiam, speculantis animus sublevetur.
candidates.englishAsRendered: so that through invisible form and the figure of invisible things the mind of the beholder may be lifted up into the understanding of intelligible things.
candidates.whyContradiction: The very next sentence states the Victorine ascent formula correctly and by explicit contrast: 'Felix cui visibilium scientia fit scala ad invisibilia cognoscenda' (happy the one for whom knowledge of VISIBLE things becomes a ladder to knowing invisible things). As printed, the first clause has the mind ascending from invisible form to invisible things — collapsing the very distinction the surrounding paragraph is built on ('visibilium speculationi speculationem invisibilium continuaret' a few lines later says the same thing correctly).

candidates.printedLatin: et omnis inferior vis animae proprio interim induitur officio.
candidates.englishAsRendered: and every lower power of the soul is meanwhile clothed with its own office.
candidates.whyContradiction: The sentence is the climax of a description of the body lying senseless in the tomb: 'Jacet hic corpus sine sensu et motu... nihil sensualitas, nihil agit imaginatio' (sensuality does nothing, imagination does nothing) — the lower powers are said to have CEASED functioning. 'induitur' ('is clothed with', i.e. is actively engaged in) its own office states the reverse of a paragraph whose entire point is that these powers are stripped of / laid aside from their office during this mystical burial.
